cards.front: What common principle explains how crawling cells and motile axonemes turn internal motion into visible movement?
cards.back: Polymers and motors generate internal relative motion; mechanical constraints and selective motor control shape that motion into edge advance or axonemal bending.
cards.quote: polymers and motors create internal relative motion, while mechanical constraints and control of which motors are active shape its visible output

cards.front: In the one-dimensional leading-edge model, edge speed = polymerization speed {{c1::− retrograde-flow speed}}.
cards.back: Polymerization is relative to the network; retrograde flow and edge speed are relative to the substrate.
cards.quote: edge speed = polymerization speed − retrograde-flow speed
cards.section: A crawling edge: measure the hidden motion

cards.front: Why must the reference frames be kept separate when calculating a crawling cell's leading-edge speed?
cards.back: Polymerization is measured relative to the actin network, whereas retrograde flow and edge motion are measured relative to the substrate.
cards.quote: Polymerization speed is measured relative to the actin network; retrograde-flow and edge speeds are measured relative to the substrate.
cards.section: A crawling edge: measure the hidden motion

cards.front: Actin polymerizes forward at 40 nm/s relative to its network, which flows rearward at 25 nm/s relative to the substrate. How fast and how far does the edge advance in 120 s?
cards.back: Speed = 40 − 25 = 15 nm/s. Distance = 15 nm/s × 120 s = 1,800 nm = 1.8 µm.
cards.quote: Edge speed = 40 + (−25) = 15 nm/s. In 120 s the edge advances 15 × 120 = 1,800 nm = 1.8 µm.
cards.section: A crawling edge: measure the hidden motion

cards.front: A leading edge advances at 15 nm/s while its actin network flows rearward at 20 nm/s. What is the polymerization speed relative to the network?
cards.back: Edge speed = polymerization − flow, so polymerization = 15 + 20 = 35 nm/s.
cards.quote: Keeping those reference frames separate gives: edge speed = polymerization speed − retrograde-flow speed
cards.section: A crawling edge: measure the hidden motion

cards.front: Polymerization remains 40 nm/s, but stronger clutch engagement reduces retrograde flow from 25 to 10 nm/s. By what factor does the 120-s edge advance change?
cards.back: Old advance = (40 − 25) × 120 = 1.8 µm. New advance = (40 − 10) × 120 = 3.6 µm. It doubles: 3.6/1.8 = 2.
cards.quote: Here, cutting flow from 25 to 10 nm/s doubles edge advance, from 1.8 to 3.6 µm.
cards.section: A crawling edge: measure the hidden motion

cards.front: Why does the one-dimensional edge-speed equation not necessarily give the speed of the whole cell?
cards.back: Whole-cell crawling also requires body movement and rear release; the equation predicts only the leading edge.
cards.quote: This one-dimensional relation predicts the leading edge, not automatically the cell body.
cards.section: A crawling edge: measure the hidden motion

cards.front: At a lamellipodium's front, actin subunits add at {{c1::barbed ends}}, the fast-growing filament ends.
cards.back: This addition pushes the membrane.
cards.quote: At its front, actin subunits add at barbed ends, the fast-growing filament ends, and push the membrane.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: What does Arp2/3 do at the leading edge of a crawling cell?
cards.back: It starts a branch from an existing actin filament, helping build the protrusive actin network.
cards.quote: The Arp2/3 complex, a seven-protein assembly, starts a branch from an existing filament.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: The small signalling switch {{c1::Rac}} helps activate Arp2/3 at the leading edge.
cards.quote: Rac, a small signalling switch, helps activate Arp2/3 there
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: What role does non-muscle myosin II play behind the front of a crawling cell?
cards.back: It forms small filaments and contracts actin. In fish keratocytes, evidence supports contraction where the lamellipodium meets the cell body as a driver of body movement.
cards.quote: Behind the front, non-muscle myosin II—a two-headed relative of muscle myosin—forms small filaments and contracts actin.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: The four processes of the crawling cycle are protrusion, grip, contraction and {{c1::release}}.
cards.back: Rear adhesions must release for the cell to advance.
cards.quote: Together, protrusion, grip, contraction and release form the crawling cycle.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: How can the timing of the four crawling processes differ between a smoothly gliding keratocyte and a fibroblast?
cards.back: They run simultaneously in a smoothly gliding keratocyte but are more cyclic in cells such as fibroblasts.
cards.quote: These four processes run at the same time in a smoothly gliding keratocyte; in cells such as fibroblasts they are more cyclic.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: What two forces contribute to retrograde actin flow in the crawling model?
cards.back: The membrane pushes back on growing filaments, and myosin II pulls the network rearward.
cards.quote: The membrane pushing back on growing filaments and myosin II pulling the network rearward both contribute to retrograde flow.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: How does actin disassembly behind the leading edge support continued protrusion?
cards.back: Disassembled filaments return monomers that can be used for growth at the front.
cards.quote: filaments that come apart a short way behind the leading edge return monomers for growth at the front.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: A cell's integrins are locked in a high-affinity state, so it grips fibronectin strongly but migrates slowly. What process is most likely limiting, and why?
cards.back: Rear release is limiting. Strong adhesions resist detachment, so better grip at the front cannot compensate for a rear that cannot let go.
cards.quote: Stronger adhesion can also slow migration by resisting rear release.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: Two regions of a PtK1 cell on a flexible, fibronectin-coated gel have different actin-flow speeds. Can you conclude that the faster-flow region exerts more traction? Why?
cards.back: No. In this PtK1 system, traction stress and local actin speed had a two-part relationship, so faster flow does not always mean more traction.
cards.quote: faster flow does not always mean more traction.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: Why can either very weak adhesion or excessively strong adhesion reduce whole-cell migration?
cards.back: Weak adhesion provides poor grip and coupling, whereas excessive adhesion can prevent rear release. Effective crawling requires both traction and detachment.
cards.quote: Strong coupling at the front cannot help if the back cannot let go.
cards.section: From edge advance to whole-cell crawling

cards.front: A classic 9+2 axoneme contains nine outer doublets surrounding {{c1::a central pair of single microtubules}}.
cards.back: Each outer doublet has a complete A-tubule fused to an incomplete B-tubule.
cards.quote: nine outer doublets, each a complete A-tubule fused to an incomplete B-tubule, surround a central pair of single microtubules.
cards.section: The axoneme: what the model predicts

cards.front: What structure anchors an axoneme in the cell?
cards.back: The basal body.
cards.quote: The ring grows from a basal body, which anchors the axoneme in the cell.
cards.section: The axoneme: what the model predicts

cards.front: In a motile axoneme, where are dynein arms anchored, and which structure do their heads grip?
cards.back: The arms sit on the A-tubule of one doublet; their heads grip the B-tubule of the neighbouring doublet.
cards.quote: Outer and inner rows of dynein arms sit on each A-tubule; their motor heads grip the B-tubule of the next doublet
cards.section: The axoneme: what the model predicts

cards.front: How does axonemal dynein move neighbouring doublets relative to one another?
cards.back: Its heads walk toward the neighbouring B-tubule's minus end at the base, pushing that neighbouring doublet toward the tip.
cards.quote: walk toward its minus end, at the base, so each doublet pushes its neighbour toward the tip.
cards.section: The axoneme: what the model predicts

cards.front: What two axonemal structures help regulate dynein and resist or coordinate sliding?
cards.back: Radial spokes help regulate dynein; the nexin-dynein regulatory complex links neighbouring doublets, resists sliding, and helps regulate motors.
cards.quote: the nexin-dynein regulatory complex links the pair, resists sliding and helps regulate the motors.
cards.section: The axoneme: what the model predicts

cards.front: How is dynein-driven sliding converted into axonemal bending?
cards.back: Interdoublet resistance and anchoring at the base prevent free sliding, converting dynein-driven shear into curvature.
cards.quote: interdoublet resistance and base anchoring similarly turn dynein-driven shear into bending
cards.section: The axoneme: what the model predicts

cards.front: Sea-urchin sperm axonemes are briefly treated with trypsin and then ATP; doublets slide out of the bundle. What does this show?
cards.back: Dynein changes the relative positions of doublets by ATP-driven sliding. With resisting structures cut, that motion appears as disintegration instead of bending.
cards.quote: Under dark-field microscopy, groups of doublets slid out of the bundle.
cards.section: The axoneme: what the model predicts

cards.front: Design a test of whether dynein motors work in a mutant with paralysed flagella.
cards.back: Isolate and demembranate axonemes, briefly cut sliding resistance with trypsin, add ATP, and test for doublet sliding against identically treated wild-type and no-ATP controls.
cards.quote: Design a test of whether its dynein motors themselves work. Isolate the axonemes first
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After trypsin and ATP, doublets from a paralysed mutant slide apart like wild type. What does this rule in, and what remains unresolved?
cards.back: At least some dynein can bind the neighbouring B-tubule, use ATP, and generate motion. A missing arm row or defects in regulation or sliding-to-bending conversion remain possible.
cards.quote: Sliding apart shows that at least some dynein arms can bind the neighbouring B-tubule, use ATP and generate motion.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A paralysed axoneme has both dynein arm rows and still shows ATP-driven sliding after trypsin. Where should you look next for the defect?
cards.back: Look in motor regulation or sliding-to-bending machinery, such as radial spokes, the central pair, or the nexin-dynein regulatory complex.
cards.quote: a paralysed but sliding axoneme probably has a defect in motor regulation or in converting sliding into bending
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mutant axonemal doublets do not slide after resistance is cut and ATP is supplied. What is the leading suspicion?
cards.back: The dynein arms may be missing or inactive, because working dynein should generate sliding under these conditions.
cards.quote: If doublets do not slide apart, suspect missing or inactive dynein arms.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why include axonemes given ATP without trypsin in a dynein sliding assay?
cards.back: They show that intact resistance normally converts internal sliding into bending or beating rather than bundle disintegration.
cards.quote: Intact wild-type axonemes given ATP should still slide internally but bend or beat rather than fall apart.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why must dynein activity be asymmetric across an axoneme to create a bend and alternate between sides to create a wave?
cards.back: Equal activity on opposing sides would not select a bending direction. A wave requires the favored side to switch over time.
cards.quote: Even a single bend needs dyneins on one side to be more active than those on the other
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Dynein arms are absent from both sperm flagella and airway cilia. Predict the cellular phenotypes.
cards.back: Sperm will not swim, and airway cilia will not beat effectively, severely impairing mucociliary transport.
cards.quote: Airway cilia that do not beat severely impair this mucociliary transport; sperm missing dynein arms do not swim.
cards.section: From a broken part to a cellular phenotype

cards.front: A mouse embryo has no cilia on its node. What happens to left-right organ placement, and why?
cards.back: Organ placement becomes randomized because the node cannot generate its normal leftward flow.
cards.quote: It becomes randomized because the node cannot make its normal leftward flow.
cards.section: From a broken part to a cellular phenotype

cards.front: Why can one ciliary mutation cause complete immotility in one tissue but only abnormal beating in another?
cards.back: Cilia share a basic machine but can differ in some dynein parts, so one mutation need not have the same effect everywhere.
cards.quote: One mutation need not have one effect everywhere.
cards.section: From a broken part to a cellular phenotype

cards.front: Conventional electron microscopy shows normal-looking ciliary dynein arms despite a motility defect. What lesson-based follow-up could reveal a subtler structural defect?
cards.back: Use three-dimensional electron tomography; it can reveal defects, such as reduced outer-arm volume near the base, that conventional images miss.
cards.quote: electron tomography found reduced outer-arm volume near the base.
cards.section: From a broken part to a cellular phenotype

cards.front: Neutrophils lack a functional β2-family integrin. Predict their migration defect and its consequence.
cards.back: They grip vessel walls poorly and largely fail to leave the blood, so infections are poorly controlled.
cards.quote: grip the vessel wall poorly and largely fail to leave the blood, so infections are poorly controlled
cards.section: From a broken part to a cellular phenotype

cards.front: Membrane bulges driven by pressure from contraction of the actin cortex are called {{c1::blebs}}.
cards.back: Blebbing is an alternative to lamellipodial clutch-based crawling.
cards.quote: Some form blebs, rounded membrane bulges driven by pressure from contraction of the actin cortex under the membrane.
cards.section: Other ways to migrate

cards.front: Why is transmembrane force coupling not essential for every migrating cell?
cards.back: Confined leukocytes can move without it by using actin flow that follows the texture of their surroundings.
cards.quote: Confined leukocytes can move without transmembrane force coupling, using actin flow that follows the texture of their surroundings
cards.section: Other ways to migrate

cards.front: Primary cilia are generally single, non-motile {{c1::9+0}} sensory organelles that lack dynein arms.
cards.back: They act as signalling antennae on many vertebrate cell types.
cards.quote: Primary cilia are single, non-motile 9+0 sensory organelles on many vertebrate cell types; they lack dynein arms and act as signalling antennae
cards.section: Cilia that bend the simple categories

cards.front: How do motile cilia near the center of the mouse embryonic node move?
cards.back: They rotate rather than wave.
cards.quote: Those near its centre move by rotating rather than waving
cards.section: Cilia that bend the simple categories

cards.front: What remains uncertain in the proposal that alternating inhibition switches active dyneins from one side of a beating axoneme to the other?
cards.back: The switching signal remains unknown; selective inhibition of one motor set is a proposal, not an established mechanism.
cards.quote: The authors suggested that the sides switch by selectively inhibiting one set of motors. This is a proposal; the switching signal remains open.
cards.section: Repeats and the switching proposal
